tracks.title: Prove the call without the phone
tracks.text: Lesson 05 point 12 — rehearsals. This one is a sub-lesson, under agents… and it answers a hard question. How do you prove a voice agent works… when the front door is a phone call? Here's the idea, up front. A rehearsal is a text self-demo of a voice-agent conversation. Scripted human lines… a live model wearing the production persona… and every single tool call routed through the real production router. No provider. No human on the line. [curious] The untested surface shrinks to exactly one hop you don't own. And the transcript… is the test. A thing you can read… diff… and commit.

tracks.title: The last hop can't be CI
tracks.text: First — the last hop can't be CI. You built an agent whose front door is something automated tests can't drive. A phone call… a voice provider… a webhook console you don't even host. Your unit tests are honest about the parts they reach — the tool code, the auth check, the ledger. But the conversation itself goes untested. [curious] Does the persona hold for a whole exchange? Does the model call repo state… instead of confidently inventing the project's status? Does the whole chain hold up when a live model — not a fixture — is the thing driving it? The usual answer is, call it and see. Which means a human on every check… and a provider key in every environment. [sighs] That's not a test. That's a chore. And it's exactly the chore that never gets done. This project's voice agent, the groundskeeper, hit this wall head-on. Voice can't be CI… because the founder isn't always on the call, and the key may not even be provisioned. So the most important layer… was the one nothing covered.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A rehearsal is a text self-demo of a voice-agent conversation. Scripted human lines drive a live model wearing the production persona… and every tool call runs through the real production router. No external service. No human. The output is a committed transcript. [excited] And here's what makes it special — a rehearsal is three things at once. First… it's a test, because a model really drives the conversation through real code. Second… it's a demo, because the side effects are real. Third… it's a document, because the result is a datestamped file you can read like any plan. Persona held… stops being a vibe. It becomes a line you can point at.

tracks.title: Cut at the last seam
tracks.text: Next — cut at the last seam. The whole idea is one decision. Where do you put the knife? Picture the conversation as a layer cake, top to bottom. At the very top sits one box, grayed out and dashed — the telephony hop. The provider's network, their voice synthesis, their webhook delivery. That's theirs. You don't own a line of it. And below it… four solid layers light up. First, in bright green — the persona and the live model. Does it hold? Does it call tools? Second — the router's auth, the secret header that fails closed. Third — the five real tool implementations. And fourth — the task ledger. A dashed arrow runs down from that grayed top box into the green one… labelled, the one hop a rehearsal can't reach. [curious] So the knife goes right under the provider. Everything below the cut is your code, and a rehearsal exercises all of it. The untested surface is as small as it can possibly be — one hop you genuinely don't own… and nothing else.

tracks.title: One line, six rounds
tracks.text: Now the mechanics — one line, six rounds. A rehearsal is a reduce over scripted human lines. You hand it a list of founder lines… and the agent side is a live model. For each line, the model completes. And if it wants tools, it calls them, the results get appended, and it completes again — up to six rounds — before it's forced to answer in plain words. Picture one exchange as a little play. A scripted human line goes to the model. Round one — the model asks the real router for repo state, the ledger reads it, and a grounded answer comes back. Round two — the model dispatches a background goal, the ledger files a task it calls gk two-oh-one, and the router confirms. After at most six rounds like that, the model is forced to stop calling tools and answer in words. And that reply… plus every tool call along the way… is written into the transcript. One detail keeps it faithful. The assistant message sent back to the model is stripped down to just role, content, and tool calls — the same echo convention the real agent loop uses. And if the model errors? The rehearsal doesn't crash. The turn just reads, open paren, llm error. So a flaky model never costs you the whole run.

tracks.title: Through the real router
tracks.text: A depth rung — skippable — the thirteen lines that make it not a mock. Here's the seam itself. When the model calls a tool, the rehearsal does not reach into a fake. It builds an in-process request and hands it to the literal router that serves production. In words — it constructs a POST to slash tool slash the tool name, with the args encoded as JSON. It sets a content-type header of application JSON… and an x-gk-secret header carrying the secret. Then it calls the real groundskeeper router. Now set that beside what the deployed provider actually sends. The provisioned webhook posts to the same base URL, slash gk slash tool slash the tool name… with the same x-gk-secret header… and the args as a JSON body. Same route. Same header. Same body schema. [excited] Only the HTTP transport differs. The rehearsal's request is built in memory instead of arriving over the wire — and from there, it's byte for byte the production path. So one rehearsal exercises, for free, everything that path touches. The constant-time secret compare that fails closed with a 503 when the secret is unset… the JSON marshalling… the five real tool implementations… and the ledger writes. Compare that to a mock. A mocked tool call skips the auth check, bypasses the marshalling, stubs a return value, and never touches the ledger. The real-router call runs all four for real. The verdict, in one line — a mock fakes everything below the call. A rehearsal fakes only the wire.

tracks.title: One def, two consumers
tracks.text: One def… two consumers. Here's a quiet but crucial point. A demo that drifts from production… isn't a demo of production. So the persona isn't retyped for the rehearsal. It's read from the same definition file the live provisioning reads. Picture one file at the top — the agent's org definition, with a heading that reads, star star System prompt. From that single source… two arrows fan out. One arrow goes to provisioning… which builds the live deployed agent. The other goes to the rehearsal… which runs the self-demo. One file. Two consumers. The personality you prove in a rehearsal is, by definition, the one production runs. And that heading is load-bearing. A definition whose prompt doesn't live under star star System prompt… parses to nothing, and the agent runs empty. [sighs] This project has actually shipped that bug before. Which is exactly why both consumers raise loudly… instead of falling through to an empty brain.

tracks.title: The transcript is the artifact
tracks.text: The transcript is the artifact. A rehearsal writes itself down. The result lands in a datestamped file under a rehearsals folder — a first-class directory of the method, sitting right beside the agent's sources and workflows. Each turn is a founder heading and a groundskeeper heading… and any tool calls follow as a list. Let me read you one real turn, from the first rehearsal that ever proved the groundskeeper. The founder asks for some background research. The groundskeeper replies — Sent it out. Task gk two-oh-one, researching E2B and Daytona pricing from their official pages, docs, and recent mentions. I'll bring it back when it lands. And then the tool calls. First, a dispatch — goal, research E2B and Daytona pricing — and the result comes back, dispatched true, task gk two-oh-one, workflow, a research org file. Second, a capture — kind, idea — about sharpening the workbook-as-container pitch… and the result, captured true, saved to a captures file. [curious] Now read what that proves. The very first reply in the run was grounded — the model called repo state before asserting anything about the project, exactly as its tool description demands. This turn shows a real dispatch — the goal went to the runtime, the task was filed, and a workflow file was written that still exists in the repo today. A six-leaf ordered outline with done-when shell gates. The captures were silent — saved, never read back. And the run ends with honesty you can see in text. A later tasks call returns finished, null… and the agent says, still working, no results back yet. [excited] No fabricated completion. That readback is observable, in plain text, forever. The workflow file persisting in the repo isn't a leak — it's the point. A rehearsal's side effects are real artifacts. Which is exactly what makes it a demo… and not a mock.

tracks.title: Where it sits on the ladder
tracks.text: Where it sits on the ladder. A rehearsal isn't the only rung — it's the middle one. And knowing its neighbors is how you read its result honestly. There are four rungs. First, at the bottom — ordinary CI. Unit tests where every model and author call is injected, so there's no network at all. They cover auth failing closed, the capture file's shape, a crash routing to blocked. Second — the rehearsal itself. A live model, the real router, the real tools, the real ledger. The only thing faked is the telephony wire. Passing it proves the conversation layer holds, end to end. Third — provider simulation. The provider runs the agent's real deployed prompt through its own text simulator. This one needs the conversation key… the very key the rehearsal deliberately does without. And fourth, at the top — a live call, with a human on the line, where everything is real and nothing is faked. [excited] So the verdict. The rehearsal is the rung where a live model meets the real router… with no provider in the loop. The most coverage you can get… for the least ceremony. It needs an ordinary model key, and no voice key at all. That's how the groundskeeper's go-live readiness was proven while still blocked on the conversation key. Shipped and proven by rehearsal. No human. No provider. Persona held. The agent went live afterward.

tracks.title: What a green rehearsal doesn't prove
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what a green rehearsal doesn't prove. Because a test you over-read… is worse than no test. Four limits. First — the telephony hop stays untested. A rehearsal passing is not voice working. And the proof of that is in the history. The missing-permission block on the conversation key… was discovered by trying to go live. Not by any rehearsal. Second — the side effects are real, and there's no dry-run. Captures land on disk, dispatches really run workflows and burn model calls, issues really file. That's a feature — it's a demo of the real thing — but it means a rehearsal dirties your repo and spends tokens every time. Third — the tool specs are hand-mirrored. The rehearsal keeps its own copy of the five tool specs… and the code's own comment admits it. That mirror can drift. If the live specs change and the copy doesn't… you'd be rehearsing a slightly different agent than you ship. And fourth — persona held is a judgment, not an assertion. A rehearsal is pass or fail by reading. Nothing in the run asserts the tone was right. A human, or a judge, has to read the transcript and say so. The asserted sibling… is a judged eval. A rehearsal is the document you'd hand the judge.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is this just mocking the conversation? No — and that's the entire distinction. Nothing below the cut is mocked. The model is live, the router is the literal production module, the tools are the real five, the ledger really writes. The only thing absent… is the provider's wire. Why a live model instead of canned replies? Because tool selection is the thing under test. Does it call repo state instead of guessing? Does it dispatch when the founder commits to work? Canned replies would assert the very answers you're trying to discover. Can I run one with no keys at all? You need a model key — not the voice key. That's the whole point of the rung. Is rehearsal a generic Workbooks verb? [chuckles] No. It's a method, shown on one agent, in roughly a hundred and forty lines… invoked host-side as a maintainer op. The value isn't a button to press. It's the recipe to copy… for your own un-testable agent. Voice… SMS… Slack… anything provider-fronted.

tracks.title: Back up to agents
tracks.text: So that's the rehearsal. A text self-demo… that cuts the conversation at the last seam you own… and writes the proof down as a transcript you can read. [curious] The way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under agents — lesson five — the construct a rehearsal exists to prove. And two neighbors fill in the recipe. Dispatch, for the spawn lane that fires task gk two-oh-one. And evals, for the judged sibling — the asserted version of a transcript a human reads. Prove the call… without the phone. That's the whole idea.
